passage: On the terrace of the old house in the hills, Aditi took her diary and said to her mother, “Amma, can I have some privacy, please?” Her mother put her hand over her heart, surprised. “What do you write in there?” “Just my own things.” Ishita, her little cousin, peeked from the doorway. “I want to see!” “No,” said Aditi, clutching the book. Her mother said gently, “Ishita, that is Aditi's. You may ask, but she can say no.” Then she added, “Keep the door open a little and tell me where you are, okay?” Aditi nodded, a bit relieved.

qa.q: Where did this scene take place?
qa.a: On the terrace of the old house in the hills.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel when she asked for privacy and her mother was surprised?
qa.a: She was probably a little nervous and wanted to keep her own thoughts to herself, and she felt relieved when her mother respected her wish.

qa.q: What limit did Aditi's mother add for safety?
qa.a: She asked that the door stay a little open and that Aditi say where she was.

qa.q: Why might Ishita have wanted to look at the diary?
qa.a: Ishita was probably curious about what her older cousin was writing, and did not yet understand that a diary is private.

grounding: A child asks for privacy with a diary, and an adult honours it while explaining a safety limit.

passage: Santiago's football team was changing after the match in a small changing room in Lima. Santiago said to the coach, “Can you please close the curtain? I want to change alone.” Kofi, a teammate, laughed, “Why? Everyone's the same!” Santiago felt his ears burn. The coach said, “That's a fair request, Santiago. Use the curtain. Kofi, everyone is allowed privacy.” Kofi shrugged. Then the coach added, “I'll be just outside, and if you need anything, call.” Santiago nodded. When he came out, he said quietly, “Thanks.” The coach nodded and waved him along to the bus.

qa.q: What did Santiago ask the coach to close?
qa.a: The curtain.

qa.q: Why did Santiago's ears burn when Kofi laughed?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed at being teased for wanting privacy, though the coach's words helped him feel his request was fair.

qa.q: What safety step did the coach add?
qa.a: He said he would be just outside and that Santiago could call if he needed anything.

qa.q: How might Kofi have seen Santiago's request?
qa.a: Kofi may have found it unusual because he felt everyone is the same, but he shrugged and accepted the coach's explanation.

grounding: A child asks for privacy while changing clothes, and adults honour it and explain a safety limit.

passage: At the swimming club, everyone changed in one big room, and Anirban hated it. On his third Saturday he stood outside the door, towel clutched to his chest, until the others had gone in. Then he found Coach Sangeeta. “Ma'am, can I change somewhere by myself? I don't like changing in front of people.” She didn't laugh or ask why. “Of course. The small room next to the office has a lock. Use it every time.” Then she added, “One rule: always tell me or the desk you're going in there, so an adult knows where you are.” Anirban nodded. The next Saturday he walked in whistling.

qa.q: Which room did Coach Sangeeta offer Anirban?
qa.a: She offered the small room next to the office, which has a lock.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling as he stood outside with his towel?
qa.a: Anirban felt uncomfortable and embarrassed about changing in front of others.

qa.q: How did Coach Sangeeta honour Anirban's request and keep him safe?
qa.a: She gave him a private room with a lock and set one rule: always tell an adult he's going in there, so someone knows where he is.

qa.q: How might Coach Sangeeta see Anirban's request?
qa.a: She treated it as a normal, reasonable wish for privacy, without laughing or asking why.

grounding: Shows a child asking for privacy while changing, and an adult honouring it while explaining a safety limit.

passage: I'm Arnab, and my big sister Nazia keeps a diary with a little lock. Last week Mummy found it lying open on the sofa and picked it up to close it. Nazia ran in, red-faced. “Please don't read it! It's private.” I thought there'd be a fight. Instead Mummy handed it straight back. “I wasn't reading. Your diary is yours.” Then she sat down. “But if something ever feels unsafe, or someone is hurting you, that's not a diary secret. Tell me.” Nazia nodded and hugged the diary. I don't know what's in it. I think Nazia trusts Mummy more now, though.

qa.q: What does Nazia's diary have?
qa.a: Nazia's diary has a little lock.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when she ran in, red-faced?
qa.a: Nazia felt alarmed and embarrassed that her private diary might be read.

qa.q: How did Mummy honour Nazia's privacy and still set a safety limit?
qa.a: She handed the diary back unread and said it was Nazia's, but explained that anything unsafe or anyone hurting her is not a diary secret.

qa.q: How does Arnab think the moment changed things?
qa.a: Arnab thinks Nazia trusts Mummy more after seeing her privacy respected.

grounding: Shows a child asking for privacy with a diary, and a parent honouring it while explaining that safety concerns must be shared.

passage: Monday: Bhavna was in the bathroom when her little brother barged in looking for his toy boat. “GET OUT!” she screamed. He cried. Rekha came running. Tuesday: At bedtime Bhavna said, quietly this time, “Amma, I need the bathroom to be private. Can there be a knocking rule?” Rekha nodded. “That's fair. You're growing up. Everyone knocks, even me. But don't slide the top bolt, so if you ever slip, I can get in.” Thursday: A tiny knock came at the bathroom door. “Didi? Is my boat in there?” Bhavna laughed. “Wait two minutes!” She handed it out, dripping, through the gap.

qa.q: What was Bhavna's brother looking for?
qa.a: He was looking for his toy boat.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling when she screamed “GET OUT”?
qa.a: Bhavna felt shocked and embarrassed at her privacy being broken.

qa.q: How did Rekha honour Bhavna's request and keep a safety limit?
qa.a: She made a knocking rule for everyone but asked Bhavna not to slide the top bolt, so Rekha could get in if she ever slipped.

qa.q: What was Thursday like for Bhavna's little brother?
qa.a: He remembered to knock and got his boat back without any shouting.

grounding: Shows a child asking calmly for bathroom privacy, and a parent honouring it with a knocking rule and a safety limit.

passage: "Ganga, you asked me to knock before coming in while you change. Good. You're right to ask. Let me, your grandmother Dolma, tell you why I agree so fast. When I was eleven, in Gangtok, I kept a diary under my mattress. One day I found my mother reading it by the window. I didn't speak to her for two days. When your mother was your age, I promised I would never read her diary. But I also told her, 'Privacy is yours, but I must always know where you are and who you're with. That part is for safety.' So: I will knock, and I won't touch your notebook. And you will tell me when you go to your friend's house. Fair?"

qa.q: Where did young Dolma keep her diary?
qa.a: Under her mattress.

qa.q: How did young Dolma feel when she found her mother reading the diary?
qa.a: Betrayed and hurt, so upset that she didn't speak to her mother for two days.

qa.q: What choice did Dolma make later as a mother?
qa.a: She promised never to read her daughter's diary, but explained the safety limit: she must always know where she is and who she's with.

qa.q: How might Ganga's mother, as a girl, have felt about Dolma's promise?
qa.a: She likely felt trusted and respected, knowing her diary was her own, while understanding why her mother needed to know where she was.

grounding: It is a grandmother's memory explaining why she honours a child's request for privacy while keeping the safety limit of knowing where she is.
